content: The Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) process at the provider level involves various elements such as job aids, supportive supervision, training follow-up, and mentorship. These measures aim to enhance the quality of care provided by healthcare professionals. At the facility level, CQI may include actions like small infrastructure modifications, changes to admission procedures, or improved signage to ensure greater privacy and confidentiality, particularly for adolescent clients. Informational materials and visual aids can assist healthcare providers in effectively communicating with adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) about their treatment and care needs. Ensuring the availability of necessary equipment and supplies is critical for the timely and appropriate delivery of services. The involvement of peer educators and lay health workers can help reduce the workload of healthcare workers while providing additional support to patients. Negative attitudes among healthcare workers disproportionately affect adolescents compared to adults, with an even greater impact on young people from key populations. Healthcare providers must develop skills to listen attentively, communicate clearly, and recognize the hesitancy and discomfort adolescents may feel when discussing their health. Training may be required to help providers better understand how to deliver such care effectively. Training for healthcare workers on HIV-related services for adolescents is urgently needed. This training should be integrated with existing programs, such as those focused on adult HIV care or adolescent health, to ensure a comprehensive approach. For example, adolescent-specific content can be incorporated into adult HIV training, or HIV-related topics can be included in adolescent health training. Pre-service training on adolescent health, ALHIV, adolescent sexual and reproductive health, and the needs of young key populations should also be prioritized. Social workers play a crucial role in supporting ALHIV, and their involvement should be considered when planning to strengthen human resources. Training should also address issues such as alcohol and substance use, harm reduction for people who inject drugs (PWID), communication skills, adherence to HIV treatment, retention in care, self-management, mental health (including coping strategies, depression, and dealing with past trauma), and disclosure of HIV status. Adolescents should be supported in disclosing their status to others, including sexual partners, to promote safer practices and HIV prevention, while prioritizing adherence to treatment and consistent condom use. Adolescents should also receive support in making decisions about having children and planning for their future, including education and employment. Training healthcare workers should focus on changing attitudes and behaviors, which requires ongoing efforts rather than a single training event. Continuous supervision and professional support are essential components of this change process. Community-based interventions and training for healthcare workers to support treatment adherence and retention in care are important, even though the evidence base for these interventions is limited. These recommendations are included in the guidance as the best judgment of practitioners and advocates, serving as a foundation for further research on implementation. The WHO Consolidated Guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection include several service delivery recommendations. For example, community-based HIV testing and counseling (HTC) with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services is recommended in generalized HIV epidemic settings. This approach complements provider-initiated testing and counseling. In high HIV prevalence settings, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated and maintained for eligible pregnant and postpartum women and infants in maternal, newborn, and child healthcare settings, with appropriate linkage to ongoing HIV care. In settings with a high burden of HIV and tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated for HIV-positive individuals with TB in TB treatment settings, with linkage to ongoing HIV care. Similarly, TB treatment should be provided for individuals with HIV in HIV care settings where TB diagnosis has been made. In settings where opioid substitution therapy is provided, ART should be initiated and maintained for eligible individuals with HIV. Decentralization of ART initiation and maintenance should be considered, including options such as initiating ART in hospitals and maintaining it in peripheral health facilities or community-based settings like outreach sites, health posts, or home-based services. Task-shifting is another strategy, where trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses can initiate and maintain ART, and trained community health workers can dispense ART between regular clinical visits. Mobile phone text messages can be used as a reminder tool to promote adherence to ART. This approach has been successfully used for other chronic illnesses among adolescents and has the potential to improve adherence and support. However, it is essential to involve ALHIV in the development of these programs. Adolescent HTC services must be voluntary, confidential, and accompanied by high-quality pre-test information and post-test counseling. Programs should ensure effective referrals to appropriate care and follow-up services. Gender issues and the specific needs of adolescent men, women, and transgender individuals must be considered in all recommendations. A human rights perspective should underpin all actions, ensuring that they are in the best interest of adolescents, as specified in the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Adolescents have the right to non-discrimination, privacy, confidentiality, and participation in decision-making processes that affect their lives.
